title: Module Overview: Classification Table and Axiom Budget
content: The module docstring serves as a compact reference sheet. The classification table (lines 32-39) is notable: it summarises the dihedral angles of all five Platonic solids and which have zero Dehn invariant. The imports reveal the proof's dependency chain: this file builds on `DissectionOfCubesOQ02` (Niven's theorem for arccos(1/3)/π) and `DissectionOfCubesOQ02OQ02` (Dehn–Sydler infrastructure: the tensor product ℝ ⊗_ℤ (ℝ/πℤ), `edgeTerm`, `tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero`). The axiom budget lists exactly 2 axioms inherited from those parent files — a tight accounting that was tracked deliberately.
mathContext: The Platonic solids are the only convex polyhedra with congruent regular polygonal faces and the same number of faces meeting at each vertex. There are exactly five (Euler's formula + regularity constraints): tetrahedron ($V=4$), cube ($V=8$), octahedron ($V=6$), dodecahedron ($V=20$), icosahedron ($V=12$). The dihedral angles are: $\pi/2$ (cube), $\arccos(1/3) \approx 70.5°$ (tetrahedron), $\pi - \arccos(1/3) \approx 109.5°$ (octahedron), $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5}) \approx 116.6°$ (dodecahedron), $\arccos(-\sqrt{5}/3) \approx 138.2°$ (icosahedron). All non-cube angles are irrational multiples of $\pi$.

title: Chebyshev Sequence Design: Clearing √5 Denominators
content: The sequence cosThreeFifthsSeq is engineered so that d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5)) is always an integer, despite cos(arccos(3/5)) = 3/5 being rational with denominator 5. Multiplying by 5^n clears all denominators from the Chebyshev evaluation: the recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n has integer coefficients 6 = 2·(6/5)·5 and 25 = 5². This parallels nivenSeq in OQ02, where multiplying by 3^n cleared the 1/3 denominator from arccos(1/3).
mathContext: For $\cos\theta = 3/5$, the Chebyshev recurrence $2\cos((n+2)\theta) = 2\cos\theta \cdot 2\cos((n+1)\theta) - 2\cos(n\theta)$ gives: $5^{n+2} \cdot 2\cos((n+2)\theta) = 6 \cdot [5^{n+1} \cdot 2\cos((n+1)\theta)] - 25 \cdot [5^n \cdot 2\cos(n\theta)]$. The key: $5^{n+2} \cdot 2\cos\theta = 5^{n+2} \cdot 6/5 = 6 \cdot 5^{n+1}$, so all factors of 5 cancel into integer coefficients. Note: `cosThreeFifthsSeq` is the `≡ nivenSeq` analog for prime 5 (the nivenSeq used prime 3).

title: Mod-5 Divisibility: Parallel to OQ02's Mod-3 Argument
content: The proof that 5 ∤ cosThreeFifthsSeq n exactly mirrors the proof that 3 ∤ nivenSeq n in OQ02. The recurrence d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} − 25d_n reduces mod 5 to d_{n+2} ≡ d_{n+1} (mod 5) — since 6 ≡ 1 and 25 ≡ 0. So the non-divisibility propagates: from 5 ∤ d_n and 5 ∤ d_{n+1}, we derive 5 ∤ d_{n+2}. The base: d_0 = 2, d_1 = 6 — neither divisible by 5. The Lean proof uses a paired induction: simultaneously proves (5 ∤ d_n) and (5 ∤ d_{n+1}) to avoid a two-step inductive step.
mathContext: If $5 \mid d_{n+2} = 6d_{n+1} - 25d_n$, then since $5 \mid 25d_n$ we get $5 \mid 6d_{n+1}$. Since $\gcd(5,6) = 1$ (5 is prime, $5 \nmid 6$), we get $5 \mid d_{n+1}$ — contradicting the inductive hypothesis. The proof uses `Prime (5 : ℤ)` and `Prime.dvd_or_dvd` to split $5 \mid 6 \cdot d_{n+1}$ into $5 \mid 6$ (false) or $5 \mid d_{n+1}$ (contradiction). This exact pattern repeats in every Niven-type irrationality argument.

title: arccos(3/5)/π is Irrational: The Cosine Identity and Final Contradiction
content: The proof `cosThreeFifthsSeq_eq_cos` establishes the arithmetic backbone: d_n = 5^n · 2cos(n·arccos(3/5)), proved by simultaneous strong induction on consecutive terms. The `cos_step` helper (from OQ02) handles the cosine addition step. The irrationality theorem `arccos_three_fifths_irrational` then proceeds by contradiction: assume arccos(3/5) = q·π for some rational q = p/q.den. Substituting n = q.den yields d_{q.den} = 5^{q.den} · 2cos(q.den · arccos(3/5)) = 5^{q.den} · 2cos(q.num·π) = ±2·5^{q.den} (since cos(mπ) = ±1). So 5 | d_{q.den}, contradicting five_ndvd_cosThreeFifthsSeq.
mathContext: The proof splits on $(-1)^{|q.\text{num}|} = +1$ or $-1$: (1) $+1$: $d_q = 2 \cdot 5^q$, so $5 \mid d_q$ via `dvd_pow_self 5` and `dvd_mul_of_dvd_right`. (2) $-1$: $d_q = -2 \cdot 5^q$, same argument. In both cases, $5 \mid d_q$ contradicts `five_ndvd_cosThreeFifthsSeq`. The Lean proof uses `exact_mod_cast` to transfer a real equation $d_n^\mathbb{R} = r$ to an integer equation $d_n = r_\mathbb{Z}$ — a common pattern when real-valued cosine identities must be reflected back to the integer sequence.

title: Half-Angle Identity: 2·arccos(1/√5) = arccos(-3/5)
content: The proof computes cos(2·arccos(1/√5)) = 2·(1/√5)² − 1 = 2/5 − 1 = −3/5, then uses Real.arccos_cos to identify the angle: since 2·arccos(1/√5) ∈ [0, π] (because arccos(1/√5) ≤ π/2, which holds since 1/√5 ≥ 0), and its cosine equals −3/5, it must equal arccos(−3/5). The key Mathlib fact: arccos_le_pi_div_two says arccos x ≤ π/2 iff x ≥ 0. The proof uses `nlinarith` to handle the nonlinear constraint from √5·√5 = 5.
mathContext: Proof: `arccos_cos(h₁: 0 ≤ 2θ)(h₂: 2θ ≤ π): arccos(cos(2θ)) = 2θ`. With $2\theta = 2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$: need $0 \leq 2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})$ (trivial) and $2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) \leq \pi$ (from $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) \leq \pi/2$ since $1/\sqrt{5} \geq 0$). Then $\cos(2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})) = 2(1/\sqrt{5})^2 - 1 = 2/5 - 1 = -3/5$ (using $\sqrt{5} \cdot \sqrt{5} = 5$).

title: Chain of Irrational Angles: 3/5 → 1/√5 → -1/√5
content: The irrationality propagates through a three-step chain. First, arccos(3/5)/π ∉ ℚ (proved via cosThreeFifthsSeq). Second, if arccos(1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(3/5)/π = 1 − 2r ∈ ℚ (using 2·arccos(1/√5) = π − arccos(3/5)), contradiction. Third, if arccos(-1/√5)/π = r ∈ ℚ, then arccos(1/√5)/π = 1 − r ∈ ℚ (using arccos(-x) = π − arccos(x)), contradiction. Each step is a simple rational arithmetic consequence. The Lean proofs of `arccos_sqrt5_irrational` and `dodAngle_irrational` each have just 4-5 lines, since the hard work was done in the Chebyshev argument.
mathContext:
Chain: $\arccos(3/5)/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$ (base) $\Rightarrow$ $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$ (via $2\arccos(1/\sqrt{5}) = \pi - \arccos(3/5)$) $\Rightarrow$ $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})/\pi 
otin \mathbb{Q}$ (via $\arccos(-x) = \pi - \arccos(x)$). If $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = r$, then $\arccos(3/5)/\pi = 1 - 2r \in \mathbb{Q}$, contradiction. If $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = r$, then $\arccos(1/\sqrt{5})/\pi = 1 - r \in \mathbb{Q}$, contradiction.

title: Applying Irrationality to Dehn Invariants: Dodecahedron and Icosahedron
content: With angle irrationality in hand, the Dehn invariant results follow a uniform two-step pattern: (1) prove the angle class has infinite order in ℝ/πℤ (`dodAngle_infinite_order`, `icoAngle_infinite_order`), (2) apply `tmul_infinite_order_ne_zero` (the flatness axiom from OQ02OQ02) to conclude the edge term is nonzero. The infinite-order step is purely algebraic: if n • [θ] = 0 in ℝ/πℤ, then θ = m·π/n for some integer m, contradicting θ/π ∉ ℚ. The icosahedron angle `icoAngle = arccos(-√5/3)` is axiomatized (the Chebyshev argument for ℤ[√5] arithmetic is deferred), but the same two-step template applies.
mathContext: $[\theta]$ has infinite order in $\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ iff $\theta/\pi$ is irrational. Proof: $n \cdot [\theta] = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ iff $n\theta \in \pi\mathbb{Z}$, iff $\theta/\pi = m/n \in \mathbb{Q}$. The flatness axiom says: if $a > 0$ and $v \in \mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ has infinite order, then $a \otimes v \neq 0$ in $\mathbb{R} \otimes_\mathbb{Z} (\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z})$. This uses the fact that $\mathbb{R}$ is flat over $\mathbb{Z}$ (equivalently, torsion-free), so tensor products with torsion-free modules cannot annihilate nonzero infinite-order elements.

title: Complete Platonic Solid Classification
content: The theorem `cube_isolated_dehn_invariant` packages the complete 5-solid classification into a single conjunction. The cube (12 edges, π/2 dihedral) has D = 0; all other Platonic solids have D ≠ 0. The tetrahedron and octahedron results come from OQ02OQ02; the dodecahedron is new in this file; the icosahedron uses the axiomatized angle irrationality. The classification has an immediate geometric consequence: no scissors-congruence exists between the cube and any other Platonic solid. `cube_unique_zero_dehn` is the strengthening: any edge-length multiple of a non-cube angle gives a nonzero Dehn invariant (3 sorries remain for general scaling lemmas, but the key `cube_isolated_dehn_invariant` is fully proved).
mathContext: Five Platonic solids (Euler: $V-E+F = 2$): Cube ($8-12+6=2$, $\pi/2$), Tetrahedron ($4-6+4=2$, $\arccos(1/3)$), Octahedron ($6-12+8=2$, $\arccos(-1/3)$), Dodecahedron ($20-30+12=2$, $\arccos(-1/\sqrt{5})$), Icosahedron ($12-30+20=2$, $\arccos(-\sqrt{5}/3)$). All non-cube angles are irrational multiples of $\pi$, giving nonzero Dehn invariants. The cube's angle $\pi/2 = \frac{1}{2}\pi$ is rational, giving $D = 0$ since $[\pi/2] = 0$ in $\mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$.
